item.title: Medical Complications of Catatonia and Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome: A Systematic Review
item.link: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S266729602600474X?via%3Dihub Medical Complications of Catatonia and Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome: A Systematic Review - ScienceDirect
item.description:
BACKGROUND : Catatonia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) are related neuropsychiatric conditions linked to diverse and potentially life-threatening medical complications; however, no large-scale review of existing literature has described the types and rates of such complications.
OBJECTIVE : We aimed to systematically examine documented medical complications associated with catatonia/NMS, delineate their clinical implications, and inform strategies for monitoring and improving patient outcomes.
METHODS : Systematic searches of PubMed and Web of Science were conducted up to February 8, 2025 for articles including patients with catatonia or NMS who experienced medical complications. Reviewers independently performed screening and data extraction. Quality assessment was completed via the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Case data were analyzed using descriptive statistics.
RESULTS : 281 articles (11 observational studies and 270 case reports/series) met inclusion criteria. Eleven observational studies examined medical complications in 2,008 patients with catatonia/NMS; study quality was low in 1, moderate in 6, and high in 4. Across studies, pneumonia occurred in 0-64% of patients, rhabdomyolysis in 0-30%, and deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolus (DVT/PE) in 0-25%, with these complications reported in both malignant and non-malignant presentations. Comparative studies identified catatonia as a significant risk factor for specific complications including DVT and rhabdomyolysis. Case reports/series (364 patients; mean age 45.7 years) demonstrated widespread complications including rhabdomyolysis (n=178), renal dysfunction (n=105), respiratory dysfunction (n=78), respiratory infections (n=47), aspiration (n=36), pulmonary emboli and infarcts (n=43), cardiac dysfunction (n=37), and malnutrition (n=63). Overall 23.9% (n=87) of case-reported patients experiencing medical complications from catatonia/NMS died. Within this case-report sample, mortality rates appeared lower among those receiving benzodiazepines (n=26, 16.9% vs n=61, 29.1%) and electroconvulsive therapy (n=6, 7.3% vs. n=81, 28.7) compared to those not receiving such interventions.
CONCLUSIONS : Catatonia/NMS carries high risks for multisystem complications and mortality, including in non-malignant cases and younger patients. Rhabdomyolysis, renal injury, respiratory compromise, and thromboembolism were particularly common. Among case reported patients, numerically lower mortality rates were seen in those who received benzodiazepines or electroconvulsive therapy. Clinicians should recognize strategies that may reduce risk for certain medical complications.

item.title: Ketamine/Esketamine in Clinical Practice : Areas of Consensus and Nonconsensus from an American Society of Clinical Psychopharmacology (ASCP) Delphi Panel Task Force
item.description: Important aspects of ketamine/esketamine treatment for mood disorders in contemporary practice remain inadequately addressed by the current evidence base, necessitating expert guidance in areas where clinical decision needs and implementation have advanced more rapidly than available data. The American Society of Clinical Psychopharmacology convened an expert task force to address unresolved questions about the practical use of these agents in "real-world" settings and potential disparities with evidence-based literature.An international panel of 21 academic mood disorder psychopharmacologist-psychiatrists with expertise in ketamine/esketamine clinical care and research.Consensus was reached on 35/105 items (33%), encompassing domains involving diagnostic conditions, contraindications, maximum dosing, racemic versus enantiomeric preparations, oral or intramuscular delivery formulations, laboratory/safety monitoring, access, and parameters for judging treatment outcome.Two successive Delphi rounds were completed alongside multiple virtual, email, and in-person meetings. Consensus was defined a priori as ≥75% agreement/disagreement on 5-point Likert survey items. All authors contributed to the interpretation and drafting of recommendations.Consensus agreement appears elusive for many key decision points involving ketamine/esketamine treatment, reflecting substantial disparities between "real-world" clinical practice and the shortcomings of the clinical trials' evidence base. Uncertainties persist regarding the use of novel formulations (eg, oral or intramuscular), high-dose ketamine infusions, ketamine-assisted psychotherapy, and use in conditions other than major depression. These areas of expert consensus and dissent lay the groundwork for future studies urgently needed to bridge the gap between evidence-based findings and treatment implementation in routine clinical settings.

item.title: Neuropsychiatric Features of Individuals With LGI1-Antibody Encephalitis
item.description:
OBJECTIVE : Leucine-rich glioma-inactivated 1 antibody (LGI1-Ab) encephalitis is one of the most common forms of autoimmune encephalitis and is associated with prominent psychiatric features. Psychiatric phenotyping of this condition has relied on small studies and has lacked detail.
METHODS : In this retrospective study, the authors reviewed the psychiatric symptomatology and clinical course among patients with a confirmed diagnosis of LGI1-Ab encephalitis.
RESULTS : The mean±SD age of the study sample (N=31) was 60.7±14.2 years; 71% of patients were men. The time to diagnosis was 4.9±5.8 months, and the follow-up time was 55.8±36.7 months. Eighteen patients had documented hyponatremia, and 22 were treated as inpatients. Psychiatric (71%), cognitive (81%), and neurological (84%) symptoms were present at similar rates, despite 97% of the patients coming from neurology referrals. Patients had a diverse range of seizures, including faciobrachial dystonic seizures. Of 19 patients undergoing detailed psychometric analysis, impairments were noted in memory or orientation (100%), executive function (63%), naming (47%), processing speed (37%), attention (32%), verbal fluency (26%), language (11%), and visuospatial abilities (11%). Patients had psychotic symptoms (42%), agitation or aggression (39%), emotional lability (35%), anxiety (26%), and subjective experiential phenomena (16%). Many patients had psychiatric sequelae that resolved after treatment, but a modest proportion of patients experienced ongoing apathy (6%), behavioral disinhibition (13%), obsessive-compulsive disorder (10%), subjective experiential phenomena (13%), and sleep disorders (29%).
CONCLUSIONS : These findings show that cognitive impairment and psychopathology are frequent in LGI1-Ab encephalitis. Future research could examine neuroimaging, psychiatric symptoms, and cognitive deficits in further detail.

item.title: Intelligence artificielle pour les revues systématiques et méta-analyses: recommandations pour un usage responsable et acceptable*
item.description: Résumé La revue systématique avec méta-analyse (RS/MA) constitue une méthode privilégiée de synthèse des preuves pour la prise de décision en santé. Mais c’est un exercice long et coûteux, dont la validité repose sur l’exhaustivité de la recherche de la littérature, la rigueur de la sélection des études, de l’extraction et de l’évaluation du risque de biais, ainsi que sur la transparence et la reproductibilité des résultats. L’essor rapide des outils d’intelligence artificielle (IA), des algorithmes déterministes aux grands modèles de langage et aux systèmes agentiques, suscite de fortes attentes (accélérer la recherche bibliographique, assister le tri des études et l’extraction des données, soutenir des méta-analyses vivantes…) autant que des risques potentiels (hallucinations, défaut de reproductibilité, dégradation de la qualité méthodologique). La table ronde n° 6 des Ateliers de Giens 2026 a réuni des experts issus des milieux académique, industriel et réglementaire afin de préciser à quelles conditions l’usage de ces outils est acceptable dans une RS/MA. Nous avons privilégié deux choix de positionnement, adoptant le point de vue de l’utilisateur final de la synthèse et privilégiant des critères d’acceptabilité plutôt que des recommandations méthodologiques. Douze recommandations sont proposées, regroupées en quatre axes : préserver la validité méthodologique ; maintenir l’humain au cœur du processus ; garantir la transparence, la traçabilité et la reproductibilité ; et favoriser un écosystème vertueux. Ces recommandations, inspirées du référentiel international RAISE et adaptées au contexte français, reflètent l’état des connaissances à la date de leur élaboration (juin 2026) dans un domaine pour lequel les outils évoluent rapidement, et ont vocation à être réactualisées.

item.title: Exploring the durability of esketamine and ketamine's antidepressant effects in the maintenance phase of treatment: A systematic review
item.description: Ketamine has shown rapid antidepressant effects in treatment-resistant mood disorders; however, the durability of these benefits during maintenance treatment remains unclear. This systematic review evaluated outcomes associated with repeated ketamine and esketamine administration during the maintenance phase of treatment. A systematic search of PubMed, Ovid, and Scopus was conducted from database inception through March 2026. Studies involving more than 8 treatments or more than 1 month of treatment in individuals with mood disorders were included. Eligible designs consisted of randomized controlled trials, open-label studies, observational cohorts, and case series. A total of 43 studies met inclusion criteria, including randomized controlled trials and extension studies (n = 8), open-label studies (n = 4), observational studies (n = 24), and case series (n = 7). Overall, ketamine and esketamine were associated with sustained clinical improvement during ongoing treatment, although outcomes varied across study designs. Randomized trials demonstrated reduced relapse rates with continued treatment, while relapse was common following discontinuation of treatment. Observational studies showed heterogeneous outcomes, with evidence of both sustained improvement and attenuation of benefit over time. Case series reported mixed durability. These findings suggest that continued treatment may be important for preserving therapeutic benefit, although long-term outcomes are not uniform across individuals. Further research is needed to optimize maintenance strategies, identify predictors of sustained response, and clarify the long-term efficacy and safety of ketamine-based therapies for mood disorders.

item.title: Mapping Individual Brain Deviations in ICD-11 Catatonia: Normative Modeling of Structural and Functional MRI Across Two Independent Cohorts
item.description:
OBJECTIVE : Catatonia is a transdiagnostic psychomotor syndrome cutting across mood disorders (MODs) and schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSDs). However, its neurobiological profiles remain poorly characterized. The authors examined structural and resting-state functional normative deviations associated with catatonia across two independent clinical cohorts, using hierarchical Bayesian normative modeling.
METHODS : Structural and resting-state functional MRI data were analyzed from two independent deeply phenotyped cohorts of 280 patients with MODs and SSDs. The Mannheim (Germany) sample included 184 patients with MODs or SSDs (58 withcatatonia), and the Bern (Switzerland) sample comprised 96 SSD patients (59 withcatatonia). Individual deviations from normative models were estimated using the PCNToolkit, based on healthy reference datasets (N=57,000 structural; N=22,000 functional).
RESULTS : Catatonia diagnosis was associated with significant ventricular enlargement (third ventricle and left and right lateral ventricles; q<0.05) and cortical thinning in the left dorsal posterior cingulate and insular cortices (q<0.05) across both cohorts. Exploratory analyses identified a significant left orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) difference between MOD and SSD patients with catatonia. In the overall catatonia versus non-catatonia comparison, the OFC association survived false discovery rate correction only in models adjusted for demographic variables. Resting-state functional analyses showed reduced connectivity between sensorimotor, salience, limbic, and executive control networks at the nominal significance level, but did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.
CONCLUSIONS : In the combined sample, catatonia was characterized by ventricular enlargement and cingulo-insular cortical thinning, supporting a transdiagnostic model implicating distributed motor-salience integration circuits. These findings provide reproducible, individual-level evidence for distributed brain network involvement in catatonia and identify candidate regions for future mechanistic and neuromodulation studies.

item.title: An Approach to Navigating the Lorazepam Challenge Test for Catatonia in Critical Care Settings
item.description: Catatonia often occurs in the setting of psychiatric illness; however, it is also found in other medical conditions, especially within critical care settings. The lorazepam challenge test (LCT) is a key diagnostic and therapeutic intervention for catatonia; however, no specific guidance exists for patients within the intensive care unit (ICU). This review synthesizes psychiatric and critical care literature to propose a structured LCT framework adapted to the ICU. Specific indications and contraindications across gradients of catatonia likelihood and medical complexity are reviewed, along with practical dosing and monitoring recommendations. An interdisciplinary collaborative workflow is also outlined along with post-LCT documentation standards. Our structured approach offers a practical foundation for future standardized protocols, education, and catatonia research in critical care.

item.title: Mapping the Mental Status Examination: Insights from a Scoping Review of Popular Psychiatry Textbooks
item.description:
OBJECTIVE : This review aims to critically examine the Mental Status Examination (MSE) as presented in contemporary textbooks used for psychiatry training and identify areas of convergence and variability.
METHODS : The authors conducted a comprehensive scoping review comprising expert sampling from top-ranked universities and a gray literature web search. Recommended textbooks available in English and published within the last decade were included. Data extraction focused on the MSE's conceptualization, structure, and definitions. Variability in the hierarchical organization and terminology was documented, internal and external consistency assessed, and a qualitative synthesis of the data performed.
RESULTS : An analysis of 12 authoritative psychiatry textbooks revealed substantial variability in the MSE's conceptualization, hierarchies, and definitions across domains, subdomains, and features. Despite agreement on the importance and purpose of the MSE, the sources lacked consensus on the MSE's fundamental nature, objectivity, and temporal scope, and did not provide explicit theoretical frameworks for their proposed structures. Problematic definitions of key terms and an absence of references to empirical literature were identified. Despite the variability, nine core MSE domains consistently emerged: Appearance, Behavior, Speech, Emotional State, Perception, Thought Process, Thought Content, Cognition, and Insight.
CONCLUSIONS : The findings underscore the need for consensus-building efforts to standardize the MSE, supported by philosophical research and empirical validation of its components. Addressing inconsistencies is crucial to ensure reliable, valid assessments in clinical practice and provide a coherent pedagogical framework for psychiatric training. A standardized MSE would enhance communication among healthcare providers, improve diagnostic accuracy, and facilitate patient care.

item.title: Multimodal Machine Learning–Based Prediction of Relapse in Major Depressive Disorder
item.description:
IMPORTANCE : Early identification of patients at high risk of relapse is key to personalized preventive strategies in major depressive disorder (MDD). However, current predictive models do not adequately account for the multimodal factors contributing to MDD relapse and fail to provide clinically meaningful predictions.
OBJECTIVE : To predict relapse within 2 years in patients with MDD by using a comprehensive machine learning pipeline that integrates an unprecedented set of multimodal data.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS : This naturalistic longitudinal prognostic study used data from the Marburg-Münster Affective Disorders Cohort Study, with baseline assessments collected from October 2014 to May 2019 and follow-up approximately 2 years later, between October 2016 and June 2021. Data analysis was conducted between July 2024 and June 2026. The study was performed at 2 sites in Germany (Marburg and Münster), with participants recruited from psychiatric inpatient and outpatient departments and the general population. Patients meeting diagnostic criteria for current or lifetime MDD without history of neurological or severe somatic conditions were included.
EXPOSURE : Natural course of illness in patients with MDD.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES : Balanced accuracy (BACC) for binary prediction of relapse vs no relapse during 2-year follow-up served as the primary outcome. Baseline features comprised 9 modalities including clinical and psychometric data, 4 structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging modalities, genetics, neurocognition, blood markers, and gut microbiome.
RESULTS : A total of 564 patients with a current or lifetime MDD diagnosis were included (367 female [65.1%]; mean [SD] age, 37.34 [13.38] years). A total of 270 patients relapsed during the 2-year follow-up, while 294 did not. Mean (SD) BACC for the prediction of relapse ranged from 47.21% (5.85%) to 64.43% (6.63%). The best-performing model was solely based on few clinical relapse risk factors, while multimodal data integration did not improve performance.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE : In this prognostic study, the models achieved moderate accuracy, yet the results suggest limited scope for guiding individual-level clinical decision-making. Predictive performance was largely driven by established clinical risk factors, indicating limited incremental value of multimodal measures when assessed at a single time point. Future advances may instead benefit from dynamic modeling approaches that more closely align temporally evolving multimodal markers with longitudinal clinical outcomes.

Effectiveness of amantadine and memantine in catatonia: A retrospective cohort study
item.description:
BACKGROUND : Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome involving motor, behavioral, cognitive, and affective dysfunction that is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. While benzodiazepines and electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) are first-line treatments for catatonia, alternative pharmacologic options are often used when response is inadequate or ECT is unavailable. N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonists, particularly amantadine and memantine, have been used as second-line agents, though evidence remains limited to case reports and small series.
OBJECTIVE : To evaluate the effectiveness of amantadine and memantine in hospitalized adults with catatonia by assessing changes in symptom severity measured by the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS). We hypothesized that these agents, when used alongside standard treatments, would generate symptom improvement.
METHODS : A retrospective study of adults hospitalized at Massachusetts General Hospital from 2016 to 2024 was conducted. Patients hospitalized with a diagnosis of catatonia who were treated with memantine or amantadine were identified from clinical records. Catatonia severity was measured using clinically documented BFCRS scores. Pre-post BFCRS changes were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with planned sensitivity analyses.
RESULTS : Fifty-seven patients received amantadine or memantine for catatonia, mostly as adjunctive treatment. One week (±2 days) after initiation, BFCRS total scores decreased by a mean of 4.9 points ( < 0.001, = 0.61). Results remained significant when excluding patients who received ECT during the first week of amantadine or memantine treatment ( = 48; mean change 5.0, < 0.001) and those with ⩾50% lorazepam-equivalent dose increases ( = 39; mean change 4.6, < 0.001).
CONCLUSION : This represents the largest cohort treated with amantadine or memantine for catatonia. Findings suggest significant symptom reduction, supporting their potential role as an adjunctive option. Prospective studies are needed to clarify predictors of response and comparative effectiveness.

item.title: Underuse of neuromodulation in depression care – Authors’ reply
item.link: https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(26)01900-8/fulltext Underuse of neuromodulation in depression care – Authors’ reply - The Lancet
item.description: En réponse à Mocking et coll., qui reprochaient à leur Seminar sur la dépression de minimiser la place de la neuromodulation, Gin Malhi et ses coauteurs réaffirment que l’ECT est un traitement efficace, fondé sur les preuves et potentiellement vital, qu’ils avaient volontairement distingué des autres techniques. Ils contestent en revanche le regroupement de l’ECT, de la rTMS, de la stimulation du nerf vague et de la stimulation cérébrale profonde sous une même étiquette de « neuromodulation », ces deux dernières restant respectivement d’usage sélectif et adjuvant ou encore expérimental. Leur critique vise surtout la rTMS, jugée insuffisamment étayée par des données de haut niveau, peu répliquée, sans phénotype clinique cible identifié et de plus en plus prescrite précocement, ses bénéfices relevant selon eux en partie d’un effet de « neuro-enchantement ». Ils soulignent enfin que la durée des cures peut retarder l’accès à des traitements efficaces et rejettent l’idée d’une sous-utilisation de la rTMS. Un échange éclairant sur le débat actuel concernant la place de la rTMS face à l’ECT dans la dépression.

item.title: Computational Analysis of Expressive Behavior in Clinical Assessment
item.description: Clinical psychological assessment often relies on self-report, interviews, and behavioral observation, methods that pose challenges for reliability, validity, and scalability. Computational approaches offer new opportunities to analyze expressive behavior (e.g., facial expressions, vocal prosody, language use) with greater precision and efficiency. This review provides an accessible conceptual framework for understanding how methods from computer vision, speech signal processing, and natural language processing can enhance clinical assessment. We outline the goals, frameworks, and methods of both clinical and computational approaches and present an illustrative review of interdisciplinary research applying these techniques across a range of mental health conditions. We also examine key challenges related to data quality, measurement, interdisciplinarity, and ethics. Finally, we highlight future directions for building systems that are robust, interpretable, and clinically meaningful. This review is intended to support dialogue between clinical and computational communities and to guide ongoing research and development at their intersection.

item.title: Lithium during maintenance electroconvulsive therapy: Secondary neuropsychological outcomes from the open-label PRASED randomized controlled trial
item.description:
BACKGROUND : Lithium is commonly used for relapse prevention after successful electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). However, the combination of lithium and ECT has warranted caution in clinical practice due to concerns about cognitive tolerability, while evidence remains inconclusive.
OBJECTIVE : To evaluate the neuropsychological effects of maintenance ECT (M-ECT), with and without lithium, in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) across all ages.
METHODS : The Preventing Relapse After Successful Electroconvulsive therapy for Depression (PRASED) study was a multicenter, open-label, randomized controlled trial. Patients who achieved remission after an acute ECT course for MDD were randomized to receive symptom driven M-ECT and maintenance pharmacotherapy with or without adjunctive lithium. In this secondary outcome analysis, neuropsychological functioning was assessed repeatedly over six months using a comprehensive test battery covering global cognition, memory, attention, fluency, processing speed and subjective memory complaints. Linear mixed-effects models were applied to examine group differences in cognitive trajectories over time and associations between serum lithium levels and cognitive outcomes.
RESULTS : No significant differences in cognitive trajectories were observed between the lithium (n = 50) and non‑lithium (n = 46) group. Neuropsychological performance improved over time in both groups across all cognitive domains except verbal fluency. Serum lithium levels were not associated with neuropsychological performance.
CONCLUSION : Lithium addition during M-ECT was not associated with impaired objective or subjective neuropsychological functioning. These findings support the neuropsychological tolerability of concurrent lithium and ECT use in the maintenance phase and may help guide treatment decisions regarding relapse prevention following successful ECT.

item.title: Irritability in the Mix: An Exploratory Study of the Role of Irritability in Characterising Mood Disorders
item.description:
OBJECTIVES : To examine the relationship between irritability and mixed states in bipolar disorder to determine how subjective irritability and mixed symptoms of mania and depression manifest in patients with bipolar disorder over a period of 18 months.
METHODS : This exploratory analysis examined longitudinal data from a randomised controlled trial of a psychological intervention for patients with bipolar disorder. Scores of subjective irritability and mood morbidity were analysed from data sampled over ten timepoints over the trial from 82 patients.
RESULTS : Significant associations were found between the presence of irritability and mixed symptoms (F(1, 684) = 20.468, p < 0.001). This relationship remained significant throughout the duration of the study and the administration of a psychological treatment which reduced both ratings of mood and irritability. Notably, when mixed symptoms are absent, irritability nevertheless remained for nearly half the time.
CONCLUSIONS : Irritability and mixed symptoms are phenomenologically linked. The persistence of this link, regardless of the existence of mixed symptoms, suggests that irritability permeates bipolar disorder and is core to its phenomenology. Future studies should interrogate the tethering of mixed symptoms and irritability in the context of bipolar disorder as this may lead to a deeper understanding of the core characteristics of the illness-both clinically and in terms of its neurobiology.

item.title: The freeze-arrest model of catatonia: a critical neuroimaging review with evo-neurobiological integration
item.description: Catatonia is a heterogeneous and poorly defined entity. Akinetic catatonia shares core phenomenology with the adaptive freeze-to-tonic immobility response, a threat-defense system conserved across evolution. It has been suggested that catatonia may be the maladaptive counterpart of the freeze-to-tonic immobility response. While similar brain structures are implicated in both entities, no theory-driven synthesis of neuroimaging evidence has been conducted to provide mechanistic support for this hypothesis. In this critical review, we cross-referenced available neuroimaging studies in human freezing and catatonia studies across etiologies. Both independent literatures implicate failure of the orbitofrontal-medial prefrontal cortices, dysregulation of the salience network, and basal ganglia-midbrain mediated motor block. Based on this review's findings, we developed the freeze-arrest model of catatonia (FAMC), a unified mechanistic framework that integrates evolutionary, neurobiological, and clinical data. The three entry points into the FAMC are overwhelming emotions, toxic-metabolic network disruption, and subcortical short-circuiting. Neurodegenerative, neurodevelopmental, and structurally mediated catatonia represent a mechanistically distinct category. FAMC is a testable evo-neurobiological model that explains the heterogeneity of acute akinetic catatonia, proposes unified diagnostic criteria, and treatment implications per presentation.

item.title: Meduna and the origins of the idea that seizures can be therapeutic
item.description: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) has been well discussed in psychiatry as one of the oldest, yet still enduring and effective treatments for several psychiatric disorders, including depression, catatonia, mania, and psychoses. However, the intellectual history of ECT is much less known in the field of epilepsy, in spite of the fact that the therapy's origins are squarely in epilepsy neuropathology. Therefore, this historical review's primary aim is to retrace the scientific roots of ECT from a uniquely epilepsy-focused perspective. We focus on the key contributions of a neuropathologist studying epilepsy, László Meduna, who was the first to wonder if seizures may be beneficial in certain psychiatric disorders. In addition, we highlight the controversies surrounding his initial results, the transition from chemoconvulsants to electrical seizure induction, and that, despite the long-standing clinical use of ECT, it is still not well understood in mechanistic terms why inducing a seizure could relieve symptoms of certain psychiatric illnesses. The history of ECT for epileptologists is particularly insightful not only because it chronicles how an idea originating from studies focusing on seizures has come to have such an enduring impact on clinical care in an area outside of epilepsy but also because it highlights how bold testing of innovative hypotheses stemming from seemingly disconnected observations can lead to tangible breakthroughs in translation.

item.title: Psychological and psychosocial interventions for treatment-resistant schizophrenia: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
item.link: https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanpsy/article/PIIS2215-0366%2824%2900136-6/fulltext Psychological and psychosocial interventions for treatment-resistant schizophrenia: a systematic review and network meta-analysis - The Lancet Psychiatry
item.description:
BACKGROUND : Many patients with schizophrenia have symptoms that do not respond to antipsychotics. This condition is called treatment-resistant schizophrenia and has not received specific attention as opposed to general schizophrenia. Psychological and psychosocial interventions as an add-on treatment to pharmacotherapy could be useful, but their role and comparative efficacy to each other and to standard care in this population are not known. We investigated the efficacy, acceptability, and tolerability of psychological and psychosocial interventions for patients with treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
METHODS : In this systematic review and network meta-analysis (NMA), we searched for published and unpublished randomised controlled trials (RCTs) through a systematic database search in BIOSIS, CINAHL, Embase, LILACS, MEDLINE, PsychInfo, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform for articles published from inception up to Jan 31, 2020. We also searched the Cochrane Schizophrenia Group registry for studies published from inception up to March 31, 2022, and PubMed and Cochrane CENTRAL for studies published from inception up to July 31, 2023. We included RCTs that included patients with treatment-resistant schizophrenia. The primary outcome was overall symptoms. We did random-effects pairwise meta-analyses and NMAs to calculate standardised mean differences (SMDs) or risk ratios with 95% CIs. No people with lived experience were involved throughout the research process. The study protocol was registered in PROSPERO, CRD42022358696.
FINDINGS : We identified 30 326 records, excluding 24 526 by title and abstract screening. 5762 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, of which 5540 were excluded for not meeting the eligibility criteria, and 222 reports corresponding to 60 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Of these, 52 RCTs with 5034 participants (1654 [33·2%] females and 3325 [66·8%] males with sex indicated) comparing 20 psychological and psychosocial interventions provided data for the NMA. Mean age of participants was 38·05 years (range 23·10-48·50). We aimed to collect ethnicity data, but they were scarcely reported. According to the quality of evidence, cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis (CBTp; SMD -0·22, 95% CI -0·35 to -0·09, 35 trials), virtual reality intervention (SMD -0·41, -0·79 to -0·02, four trials), integrated intervention (SMD -0·70, -1·18 to -0·22, three trials), and music therapy (SMD -1·27, -1·83 to -0·70, one study) were more efficacious than standard care in reducing overall symptoms. No indication of publication bias was identified.
INTERPRETATION : We provide robust findings that CBTp can reduce the overall symptoms of patients with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, and therefore clinicians can prioritise this intervention in their clinical practice. Other psychological and psychosocial interventions showed promising results but need further investigation.
FUNDING : DAAD-ASFE.

item.title: Diagnosing autoimmune encephalitis in psychiatry: clinical recommendations and unresolved challenges from the GENERATE network
item.description: Psychiatric syndromes can be caused by underlying autoimmune encephalitis (AE). This represents a diagnostic challenge at the interface of psychiatry and neurology. While AE mostly manifests with a combined, complex neuropsychiatric syndrome, some patients with AE may (initially) present with predominant or isolated psychiatric symptoms. These cases can be difficult to classify, and diagnostic approaches vary considerably across clinical settings. This paper from the GErman NEtwork for Research on AuToimmune Encephalitis (GENERATE) provides interdisciplinary expert recommendations from psychiatry and neurology for the diagnostic evaluation of patients with suspected AE as the cause of psychiatric syndromes for psychiatric care settings. It integrates current scientific evidence with practical, empirical considerations from routine clinical care in different healthcare settings. The proposed diagnostic approach to detect psychiatric manifestations of AE emphasizes a rational, stepwise evaluation incorporating clinical assessment, magnetic resonance imaging, electroencephalography, blood testing, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and neuronal/glial antibody testing in serum and CSF. In diagnostically ambiguous individuals, [¹⁸F]fluorodeoxyglucose positron-emission-tomography and advanced antibody testing (e.g., live-cell-based assays) or neuroimaging techniques (e.g., volumetric analysis) may provide additional supportive information. Typical findings and limitations of diagnostic modalities are discussed to facilitate appropriate interpretation and to avoid under-recognition or overdiagnosis. Importantly, these recommendations do not aim to define new disease entities or diagnostic criteria, but rather to support a harmonized and pragmatic diagnostic approach to patients presenting with psychiatric syndromes suspected to be caused by underlying AE. Finally, key unresolved issues in this evolving field of immunopsychiatry are outlined, and promising research strategies are described.
